However, coding `substantive_direction` as `"Favourable"` by elevating the partial Organization-only block model (Table 3, Col. 3) as the "primary estimate" inverts the authors' explicit hierarchy in Section 3.5 (p. 6), which designates the comprehensive Combined model (Table 3, Col. 5; Figure 3, p. 9) as their primary model—where `Form of government` is statistically null (`b = -1.03`, SE `0.76`, `p >= 0.10`) once major confounders such as population scale (`b = -2.08***`) and surface water (`b = 5.50***`) are controlled. `Form of government` is likewise null at the 5% level across all four models in Appendix Tables A1 and A2 (pp. 12–13: `b = -1.308` and `-1.138` in Table A1; `b = -1.903*` [`p < 0.10`] and `-1.420` in Table A2), and the authors omit mayor-led governance completely from the Abstract (p. 1), Discussion (pp. 8–9), and Conclusion (pp. 9–10). Moreover, co-estimated Family C institutional and organizational predictors in the primary Combined model (Table 3, Col. 5, p. 8) show conflicting results: wholesale `Purchased water` dependence significantly increases monthly bills (`b = 2.86**`, SE `0.91`, unfavourable), larger municipal scale (`Logged population`, discussed on p. 10 as evidence against extreme decentralization) lowers bills (`b = -2.08***`, SE `0.41`), and `Government size` (`b = 0.026`, SE `0.072`) and `SDWA` health violations (`b = 0.96`, SE `0.86`) are null. Finally, although monthly household bills for 6,000 gallons (`Water cost`, p. 6) directly measure out-of-pocket water prices (`higher = worse`), the authors caution (pp. 2, 3, 9) that nominal bills lack an income denominator and that lower rates—including mayors resisting rate hikes regardless of infrastructural needs—can signal chronic underinvestment and deferred maintenance rather than genuine affordability protection.

raw_response.polarity_or_orientation_issue: Step-by-step trace: (1) Exposure orientation: `Form of government` is coded `1` = municipality with an elected Mayor and `0` = manager/council or other non-mayor forms (Table 2, p. 6), matching `"as reported"`, though whether mayor-led vs. professional council-manager governance represents stronger institutional accountability is theoretically contestable because the authors hypothesize (p. 3) that elected mayors resist unpopular rate hikes `"regardless of infrastructural needs"`. (2) Outcome polarity: `Water cost` is the nominal monthly bill in USD for 6,000 gal of drinking water, so in immediate household expenditure terms `"higher = worse"` (a negative coefficient `-` indicates lower bills). However, the authors explicitly warn (pp. 2, 9–10) that `Water cost` is unadjusted for household income and reflects utility cost recovery for capital/maintenance needs, meaning lower bills may indicate infrastructure underinvestment and reduced long-term reliability rather than pro-affordability performance.
